items.proposedAnswer: The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site; at a high substrate concentration the substrate outnumbers the inhibitor and occupies most active sites, so the inhibition is overcome.

items.proposedAnswer: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm after karyokinesis. Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell, while plant cells form a cell plate in the centre that grows outward.

items.q: Why is meiosis essential in sexually reproducing organisms?
items.proposedAnswer: It halves the chromosome number in gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, keeping it constant across generations, and it creates variation through crossing over.

items.proposedAnswer: The shoot tip makes auxin that moves down and inhibits growth of axillary buds (apical dominance). Removing the tip removes this auxin, so the lateral buds grow into branches.

items.q: How does the seed habit help plants to survive better than spore-producing plants?
items.proposedAnswer: A seed protects the embryo with a seed coat, contains stored food for the young plant, and has a dormant state that helps it survive unfavourable conditions and be dispersed; it also frees fertilisation from the need for water.

items.proposedAnswer: Arthropods have a chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages and a segmented body with an open circulatory system; they are bilaterally symmetrical and have a haemocoel.

items.q: Birds and mammals are called homeotherms. What does this mean and how does it help them?
items.proposedAnswer: They keep a constant body temperature irrespective of the surroundings; this lets them stay active and live in a wide range of habitats, hot or cold.

items.q: Differentiate between a simple leaf and a compound leaf with one example of each.
items.proposedAnswer: In a simple leaf the lamina is entire or incised but not cut to the midrib, as in mango; in a compound leaf the incisions reach the midrib or petiole, breaking the lamina into leaflets, as in neem.

items.q: What are bulliform cells? How do they help a grass leaf survive water shortage?
items.proposedAnswer: Bulliform cells are large, empty, colourless cells in the upper epidermis of grass leaves. When they lose water the leaf curls inward, reducing the surface exposed and so lowering water loss.

items.q: How do intercalated discs help the heart to work as a unit?
items.proposedAnswer: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and contain gap junctions that let the impulse pass quickly from cell to cell, so that all the cells contract almost together.

items.proposedAnswer: The plasma membrane has a lipid bilayer, so non-polar, lipid-soluble substances dissolve in it and pass through; polar molecules and ions are repelled by the hydrophobic core and need carrier or channel proteins.

Describe the structure of a nucleotide and how a polynucleotide chain is formed.
items.proposedAnswer: A nucleotide is a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. Nucleotides join through phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one and the sugar of the next, forming a polynucleotide.

items.q: Using the idea of the transition state, explain how an enzyme speeds up a reaction.
items.proposedAnswer: The substrate must reach a high-energy transition state before turning into product, which needs activation energy. The enzyme binds the substrate at its active site and stabilises the transition state, lowering the energy barrier so the reaction is faster, but the energy difference between substrate and product is unchanged.

items.q: Give three differences between mitosis and meiosis.
items.proposedAnswer: Mitosis occurs in somatic cells and has one division giving two identical diploid cells with no crossing over; meiosis occurs in germ cells, has two divisions, gives four haploid cells and includes crossing over.

items.proposedAnswer: In C4 leaves, large bundle sheath cells form a ring around the vascular bundles with mesophyll cells outside. CO2 is first fixed in mesophyll as a four-carbon acid, which moves to the bundle sheath where it releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle, concentrating CO2 near RuBisCO.

items.proposedAnswer: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 gives 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + energy (about 38 ATP in the textbook account).

items.proposedAnswer: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. It is the first step in both, converting glucose to pyruvic acid; later steps differ, as pyruvate goes to the Krebs cycle with oxygen or to fermentation without it.

items.q: Why is water considered the most important external factor for plant growth?
items.proposedAnswer: Water gives the turgidity needed for cell enlargement, is the medium for enzyme action and nutrient transport, and is a raw material in metabolism; growth stops when water is scarce.

items.proposedAnswer: Emulsification is the breaking of large fat globules into very small droplets so that lipase can act on a large surface area. Bile salts from the liver do this.

items.q: CO2 is about 20 to 25 times more soluble than O2 in water. How does this affect its diffusion across the alveolar membrane?
items.proposedAnswer: Because CO2 dissolves much more easily in the membrane and fluids, a small difference in partial pressure is enough for it to diffuse as fast as oxygen does across the diffusion membrane.

items.proposedAnswer: Forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus) for thinking and sensation; midbrain for visual and auditory reflexes; hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla) for balance and for control of breathing and heartbeat.

items.q: Explain briefly how the loop of Henle and vasa recta help to produce concentrated urine.
items.proposedAnswer: The two limbs of the loop of Henle and the vasa recta run in opposite directions, forming a counter-current that builds a rising osmotic gradient of NaCl and urea in the medullary interstitium; water leaves the collecting duct into this gradient, concentrating the urine.
keyPoints: Counter-current flow in the loop and vasa recta
Water reabsorbed from the collecting duct

items.proposedAnswer: A taxon is a group of organisms of any rank in classification. Examples: the class Mammalia or the genus Homo.

items.q: Why do organisms placed in the same genus share more characters than organisms placed in the same family?
items.proposedAnswer: A genus is a lower category than a family. As we go down the hierarchy, the number of shared characters increases, since a genus contains more closely related species while a family includes several genera with greater differences.
keyPoints: Genus is a lower rank than family

items.q: Explain the ecological importance of bryophytes.
items.proposedAnswer: Bryophytes are pioneer colonisers of bare rock; on dying they decompose and help form soil for higher plants. They also form dense mats that hold water and prevent soil erosion.

items.q: Why is an earthworm called a segmented coelomate?
items.proposedAnswer: Its body is divided into many similar segments (metamerism) and has a true coelom, a body cavity lined by mesoderm on all sides.

items.q: Explain how the structure of guard cells makes the opening of a stoma possible.
items.proposedAnswer: The inner wall of each guard cell next to the pore is thick and less elastic, and the outer wall is thin. When the cells become turgid the thin outer walls bulge outward and pull the inner walls apart, opening the stoma; when they lose water the stoma closes.
keyPoints: Inner wall thick, outer wall thin

items.q: Why do frogs undergo hibernation and aestivation?
items.proposedAnswer: Frogs are poikilothermic and cannot regulate body temperature. To escape extreme cold in winter (hibernation) and extreme heat in summer (aestivation), they hide in burrows and become inactive.

items.q: What is the endomembrane system? Why are mitochondria not included in it?
items.proposedAnswer: It is a group of membranous organelles whose functions are coordinated and which exchange material through vesicles: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria are not included because their functions are not coordinated with these organelles.

items.q: Explain the effect of temperature on the activity of an enzyme.
items.proposedAnswer: Activity increases with temperature up to an optimum, as molecules move faster. Beyond it the enzyme is denatured and loses its shape and activity. Low temperature makes the enzyme temporarily inactive.

items.proposedAnswer: Interphase is the period between two successive M phases. G1: cell grows and prepares for DNA replication; S: DNA is replicated; G2: proteins are made and the cell prepares for mitosis.

items.q: Explain how crossing over helps in producing variation.
items.proposedAnswer: In pachytene, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments at recombination nodules. This gives chromatids with new combinations of alleles, so that the gametes carry combinations of genes not present in either parent.

items.proposedAnswer: It packages materials to be delivered to the intracellular targets or secreted, modifies proteins and lipids (for example glycosylation), forms glycoproteins and glycolipids, and forms lysosomes.

items.q: A cell that makes large quantities of protein has a very prominent nucleolus. Explain.
items.proposedAnswer: The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis and ribosome assembly, so a cell making much protein needs many ribosomes and has an enlarged, active nucleolus.

items.q: Write three differences between DNA and RNA.
items.proposedAnswer: DNA has deoxyribose sugar, thymine as a base and is usually double-stranded; RNA has ribose sugar, uracil in place of thymine and is usually single-stranded.

items.q: What is denaturation of a protein? Why does boiling an egg cause it?
items.proposedAnswer: Denaturation is the loss of the secondary, tertiary or quaternary structure of a protein, usually by heat or extreme pH, without breaking peptide bonds. Heat unfolds the egg white proteins, so they change shape irreversibly and the egg turns solid.

items.q: Cells of the adult heart and nerve tissue remain in G0. What does this mean and what is its consequence?
items.proposedAnswer: G0 is a quiescent stage in which cells leave the cell cycle and do not divide. Such cells remain metabolically active but cannot replace themselves when damaged, so damage to heart or nerve cells is not easily repaired.
keyPoints: Cells exit the cycle, no division

items.q: Differentiate between the C3 and C4 pathways with reference to the first product and the site of the Calvin cycle.
items.proposedAnswer: In the C3 pathway the first stable product is the three-carbon 3-PGA, and the Calvin cycle occurs in mesophyll cells. In the C4 pathway the first product is the four-carbon OAA formed in mesophyll, and the Calvin cycle occurs in bundle sheath cells.
keyPoints: Calvin cycle in mesophyll or bundle sheath

items.q: What is the compensation point? Why can a plant not grow if it stays at this point?
items.proposedAnswer: It is the light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so there is no net gain of food. Without a surplus of sugar, the plant cannot make new tissue for growth.

items.q: Why does oxidation of FADH2 yield fewer ATP molecules than that of NADH?
items.proposedAnswer: FADH2 passes its electrons into the chain at complex II, bypassing complex I, so fewer protons are pumped across the membrane and less ATP is produced (2 ATP against 3).
